title: Read and write files
goal: Move data between pandas and common local file formats.
prerequisites: Know DataFrame construction, column selection, and paths.

cells.title: Read and export CSV
cells.explanation: CSV stores text rows separated by delimiters. read_csv creates a DataFrame and attempts to infer column types. to_csv writes the selected data; index=False avoids saving the pandas row index as an extra column.
cells.code:
df = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "students.csv", dtype={"Student_ID": "string"})
result = df.loc[df["Score"].ge(85), ["Student_ID", "Name", "Score"]]
result.to_csv(OUTPUT_DIR / "high_scores.csv", index=False)
print(result)
print("Saved outputs/high_scores.csv")

questions.answer: A platform-independent path to a file inside the data directory.

questions.prompt: How many students score at least 85?
questions.answer: 4 students: S001, S003, S006, and S010.
IDs are labels, not quantities; text preserves formats such as leading zeros.

cells.task: Read only Student_ID, Name, and Attendance. Save students with Attendance below 85 to attendance_followup.csv.
cells.hint: Use usecols when reading and .lt(85) when filtering.
cells.solution:
df = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "students.csv", usecols=["Student_ID", "Name", "Attendance"], dtype={"Student_ID": "string"})
result = df.loc[df["Attendance"].lt(85)]
result.to_csv(OUTPUT_DIR / "attendance_followup.csv", index=False)
print(result)
cells.solution_note: The report contains S004, S008, and S011. All written files go in outputs.

options: To omit the pandas row index
check.feedback: The row index is otherwise written as an additional CSV field.

cells.watch: CSV does not preserve every pandas dtype. Check types and missing-value rules when reloading.
cells.takeaway: Inspect imports and choose export columns deliberately.

cells.title: Move records through JSON
cells.explanation: JSON can store a list of records, each represented by a dictionary. orient="records" makes this structure explicit. Re-reading a file checks that the exported shape matches what you intended.
cells.code:
df = pd.read_json(DATA_DIR / "students.json", orient="records")
result = df[["Student_ID", "Campus", "Score"]].head(3)
result.to_json(OUTPUT_DIR / "student_preview.json", orient="records", indent=2)
print(result)
print((OUTPUT_DIR / "student_preview.json").read_text())

questions.prompt: What does one JSON record represent?
questions.answer: One student row, with column names as dictionary keys.

questions.prompt: Why inspect the exported JSON as text?
questions.answer: It shows the actual file structure, not only its DataFrame representation.

cells.task: Export Student_ID and Program for the first two students, then read the saved JSON back into result.
cells.hint: Write with orient="records" and read with the same orientation.
cells.solution:
df = students().head(2)[["Student_ID", "Program"]]
path = OUTPUT_DIR / "program_preview.json"
df.to_json(path, orient="records", indent=2)
result = pd.read_json(path, orient="records")
print(result)
cells.solution_note: The round trip preserves these two records and their field names.

check.feedback: Each output dictionary describes a row using field names and values.

cells.watch: File formats can change date and nullable dtype representations; a round trip needs validation.
cells.takeaway: Choose a file orientation that matches the receiving system.

cells.title: Select an Excel worksheet
cells.explanation: An Excel workbook can contain several sheets. sheet_name selects one by name. The openpyxl engine handles the provided .xlsx workbook and is listed in the installation requirements.
cells.code:
df = pd.read_excel(DATA_DIR / "students.xlsx", sheet_name="Students", engine="openpyxl")
result = df.groupby("Campus", as_index=False)["Score"].mean()
result.to_excel(OUTPUT_DIR / "campus_report.xlsx", sheet_name="Summary", index=False, engine="openpyxl")
print(result.round(2))

questions.prompt: What is the difference between the file and the sheet?
questions.answer: students.xlsx is the workbook file; Students identifies a worksheet inside it.

questions.prompt: How many rows are in the summary?
questions.answer: 2, one for Dubai and one for RAK.

questions.prompt: Why use a new output filename?
questions.answer: It preserves the supplied source data and clearly identifies the generated report.

cells.task: Read the Students sheet. Store a summary in result with columns Program and Students, where Students counts rows per program. Export it to program_counts.xlsx, sheet Counts.
cells.hint: groupby("Program").size() counts rows; name the count column.
cells.solution:
df = pd.read_excel(DATA_DIR / "students.xlsx", sheet_name="Students", engine="openpyxl")
result = df.groupby("Program").size().rename("Students").reset_index()
result.to_excel(OUTPUT_DIR / "program_counts.xlsx", sheet_name="Counts", index=False, engine="openpyxl")
print(result)
cells.solution_note: The workbook contains two counts: six AI students and six IT students.

check.feedback: sheet_name identifies which worksheet to read or create.

cells.watch: If openpyxl is missing, install the provided requirements before running this cell.
cells.takeaway: Excel I/O needs a workbook path and the correct worksheet.

cells.title: Query a small SQLite table
cells.explanation: SQL retrieves data from tables using a query. This example creates a temporary in-memory database from the fictional data. The parameter placeholder passes a value separately from the query text.
cells.code:
with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as connection:
    students().to_sql("students", connection, index=False, if_exists="replace")
    result = pd.read_sql_query(
        "SELECT Student_ID, Name, Score FROM students WHERE Score >= ? ORDER BY Score DESC",
        connection, params=(85,))
print(result)

questions.answer: The database exists in memory for this connection and is not a disk database file.

questions.prompt: Why use a placeholder and params?
questions.answer: It passes values safely without manually inserting them into SQL text.

cells.task: Use SQL to calculate mean Score and student count for each Campus. Store the returned DataFrame in result with columns Campus, Mean_Score, and Students, ordered by Campus.
cells.hint: Use GROUP BY Campus with AVG(Score) AS Mean_Score and COUNT(*) AS Students.
cells.solution:
with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as connection:
    students().to_sql("students", connection, index=False, if_exists="replace")
    result = pd.read_sql_query(
        "SELECT Campus, AVG(Score) AS Mean_Score, COUNT(*) AS Students FROM students GROUP BY Campus ORDER BY Campus",
        connection)
print(result.round(2))
cells.solution_note: This performs the grouping inside SQL and returns the two-row result as a DataFrame.

check.feedback: The query result becomes a pandas DataFrame.

cells.watch: Only use if_exists="replace" here on the temporary classroom table; on a real database it replaces the existing table.
cells.takeaway: Pandas can receive SQL results without loading every source row.
